public_rationale: Teach Mode was unavailable to ordinary buyers at launch: Rabbit's March 26, 2024 documentation placed public release later that year, and Tom's Guide's May 1 review still listed it as a future upgrade [e1, e3]. April testing reported by Tom's Guide on May 1 and The Verge on May 2 documented repeated failures in Uber and DoorDash actions, supporting the claim that the delivered action-taking system was unreliable at launch [e2, e3]. Successful April 24 demonstrations and some successful actions in independent testing show that the system could work, but do not establish dependable operation [e2, e3, e4].
limitations: The launch reviews do not establish a representative task-success rate across users and devices [e2, e3].
The tests do not isolate failures in the underlying model from failures in integrations, interfaces or third-party services, or establish that no LAM existed [e2, e3].
The assessment concerns the April 2024 launch through May 6; the cited evidence does not establish later reliability.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: The Rabbit R1 launched without key features, including Teach Mode and a stable, reliable version of its Large Action Model.

statement.excerpt: And all of this is deeply relevant at a time when Rabbit’s R1 device has launched without several key features, such as “Teach Mode” and a stable, reliable version of its alleged “Large Action Model.”

from_speaker: has launched without several key features
a stable, reliable version of its alleged “Large Action Model.”
our_interpretation: Launch means the initial consumer release in April 2024, assessed through the May 6 post. The target period begins at the month boundary because the claim supplies no launch day.
Teach Mode being absent means ordinary buyers could not use it. A demonstration or restricted test does not establish general availability.

Stable and reliable means advertised service actions worked dependably in ordinary use. Repeated failures to complete basic supported tasks count against reliability; occasional successes do not establish it.
The LAM wording concerns the delivered action-taking experience. It does not require proving that no underlying model existed or identifying which component caused each failure.
The two named features define the checkable scope. No additional numerical requirement is inferred from 'several'.
criteria.support_condition: Launch documentation and contemporary testing establish that Teach Mode was unavailable to ordinary buyers and that advertised LAM service actions repeatedly failed in ordinary use.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence establishes that Teach Mode was available to ordinary buyers at launch and that advertised LAM actions worked consistently in ordinary use. If only one named component is established and the other is refuted, the result is mixed.

evidence.locator: Section 'What is Teach Mode, and when will we see that?', second paragraph
evidence.explanation: Rabbit placed public Teach Mode availability after the initial release and described possible preliminary insider testing. This is prelaunch documentation, corroborated by the launch-period review in e3.

evidence.locator: Section 'On the LAM', paragraph describing Uber and DoorDash attempts
evidence.explanation: David Pierce's launch-period testing found repeated failures to complete Uber and DoorDash requests, alongside unreliable Spotify behavior. These firsthand results support the ordinary reading that the delivered action system was not dependable.

evidence.locator: Section 'Uber and DoorDash integration', third paragraph; also sections 'AI generated images' and 'Verdict'
evidence.explanation: Mark Spoonauer reports repeated ride-booking and food-ordering errors, and lists Teach Mode among future upgrades, corroborating both components. He also reports successful music playback and earlier image generation, which limits the claim to unreliability rather than total nonfunctionality.
